conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists taking care of you. You were admitted for a flare of your Crohn’s disease. Can you tell me about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it started a couple nights ago. I was having about 12 bowel movements a day, which is my usual, but then suddenly it got worse. I was up every half hour all night with watery diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned pain—where is it located?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mainly in the left upper side. It gets worse when I have to go. Feels like a squeezing, crampy pain. I also had a fever at home and felt really weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for that. We gave you IV steroids in the ER to help calm the inflammation. We’ve also started IV fluids because you’ve been losing a lot through diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I took more prednisone at home—up to 35 mg—but it didn’t help much. And lomotil didn’t stop the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. When flares are this severe, oral meds often aren’t enough. We’re giving you IV methylprednisolone now, which is stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are we checking for infections? I didn’t eat anything strange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, excellent question. We sent stool tests for C. diff, parasites, and common bacteria like Salmonella. So far, all negative. That supports this being a flare, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But the pain is still pretty bad. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given IV Dilaudid, and you’re on a PCA pump so you can control it. We’re being careful because narcotics can slow the gut, but we want you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling kind of dizzy too. Is that from the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely from dehydration. Your blood pressure was low when you came in. The IV fluids should help with that over the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray this afternoon. No signs of blockage or free air, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I still feel bloated. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, inflammation can cause that. We’re keeping you NPO—no food—for now to let your bowel rest. We’ll start clear liquids once things settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your white count is elevated, which fits with inflammation. Your kidney function was a bit off—creatinine up to 1.3—but that’s improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidneys have been an issue before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s acute and likely due to dehydration. It’s already coming down. We’ll keep monitoring, but no long-term damage expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really anxious. The steroids make me feel wired, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ve consulted Psychiatry. They recommend low-dose Seroquel at night to help with sleep and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another X-ray early this morning. There’s some new dilation in the small bowel, especially on the left side. Could be a partial obstruction from inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but not an emergency. We’re not seeing signs of perforation. We’ll do a CT scan today to get a better look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. Good news—no abscess, perforation, or blockage. The area around your anastomosis is thickened, but it’s not worse than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just inflammation, not a new problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your Crohn’s is active there, but no surgical issue. We also noticed your spleen is larger than last time. We’ll follow that up with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately, but it needs monitoring. It can happen with chronic inflammation. Your PCP and GI will keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on IV Imuran—azathioprine. It’s a steroid-sparing agent to help get you off high-dose prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried that before, right? I think my kidneys didn’t like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but that was years ago. We’ll start low and monitor your labs closely. It’s important for long-term control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try some food? I’m tired of just IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try clear liquids. But go slow—your gut’s been resting. If you push too fast, it could flare again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some broth and then my pain got worse. And I’ve had more bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we were worried about. We’ll hold off on advancing your diet for now. Bowel rest is still important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bowel movements have decreased—from over 20 at home to about 6 per day. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I feel stuck here. I think I can manage better at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but we’re not quite ready to discharge. We need your pain and diarrhea more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking—I want to go home today. I know it’s against advice, but I’ll follow up with my GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But leaving AMA means the flare could worsen—risk of dehydration, hospitalization, or complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know the risks. I just need to be at home. I’ll take my meds and come back if it gets bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll discharge you with a plan. You’ll take prednisone 40 mg daily, Imuran 75 mg, Protonix, and opium tincture for diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the Seroquel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one tablet twice a day as needed, especially at night. And loperamide if the opium isn’t available yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI in one week, primary care in two. We’ve scheduled both. Call us if pain, fever, or bloody stools return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll stay on top of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be here if you need us. Take care, and good luck at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists looking after you. You were admitted through the ER with fever and abdominal pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was feeling okay until about 36 hours ago. I went out for breakfast, and when I got home, I had a sore throat and low-grade fever—around 100.7. Then my stomach pain came back, like my usual Crohn’s flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve been on prednisone and Imuran since your last admission. Any changes in your bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. Still loose, but not worse than usual. No blood. But the pain is sharper now, especially in the upper left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals were stable in the ER. We checked your labs and found your creatinine was elevated at 1.6, which suggests your kidneys aren’t filtering as well. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. That happened last time too. Is it dehydration again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, especially with your chronic diarrhea. We’re correcting it with fluids. We also gave you a dose of IV steroids in the ER to calm the Crohn’s flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been on steroids for years. They help, but I hate the side effects—especially the anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your Seroquel for anxiety. We’ll monitor how you’re feeling. We also tested your throat for strep and flu—both came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? Just a cold?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a mild viral illness, but we’re being cautious because you’re on immunosuppressants. We’ll keep an eye on your fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the belly pain? Is it just the Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered a CT scan. It shows the area where your intestine was reconnected—ileosigmoid anastomosis—still has some thickening and inflammation, but no abscess or blockage. It’s consistent with a flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. That part always hurts. But I’ve also been peeing a lot and noticed some blood. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We did an ultrasound of your kidneys because of the blood in your urine. You have an 8mm stone in the lower part of your right kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh great, another kidney stone. Is that why my back and side hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be contributing. The stone isn’t blocking the flow, so urology says no procedure is needed now. We’ll manage the pain and encourage fluids to help it pass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. So Crohn’s flare, kidney stone, and a little virus. That’s a lot at once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re addressing each. You’re on IV fluids, IV steroids every 8 hours, and we’ll keep your pain under control. We also checked your stool—no infections like C. diff, Salmonella, or parasites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried it might be something I ate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your creatinine improved to 1.4. That’s a good sign the fluids are helping your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m feeling a bit better too. The pain isn’t as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a flexible sigmoidoscopy today to look at the anastomosis site and take biopsies to confirm it’s a flare and not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? I’ve had it before, but it’s not fun.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation, so you’ll be comfortable. It’s important to make sure the inflammation is from Crohn’s and not something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scope is done. We saw deep ulcers and a cobblestone appearance at the anastomosis—classic for Crohn’s flare. Biopsies confirm active inflammation. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely Crohn’s. No surprises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re continuing IV steroids. Your pain team also wants to help with your chronic pain. They’re starting a Dilaudid PCA pump so you can control breakthrough pain safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I like that idea. I don’t want to be in pain, but I don’t want to be drowsy either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PCA lets you dose carefully. We’ll also start Flexeril, a muscle relaxant, to help with abdominal tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 1.2, which is back to your baseline. Great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start eating regular food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re upgrading you to a regular diet. We’ll watch how you tolerate it. Your fever is gone, and your pain is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m tired of broth. What about the antibiotics? You mentioned them yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even though tests are negative, because you had a fever and are immunosuppressed, we’re starting ciprofloxacin for 10 days as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it can cause nausea or tendon issues. Let us know if you have pain in your heels or joints.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re switching you from IV to oral steroids—prednisone 20mg daily. You’ll taper it down over the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know the drill. I just hope this flare doesn’t last long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident it’s under control. Your GI doctor wants to see you in two weeks. We’re also sending you home with a short supply of long-acting morphine and MS Contin for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just for a couple days, right? I don’t want to get dependent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—only for two days. You’ll continue Flexeril and your regular Protonix for reflux. And don’t forget the rectal foam for the inflammation at the anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s labs are excellent—creatinine 1.2, white count normal. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call or come back if you get fevers, vomiting, bloody stools, or severe pain. Also, don’t drive while on the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll follow up with my PCP for labs and with pain clinic about the Flexeril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll have your discharge papers ready by noon. You’ll get prescriptions for everything, including the cipro and the steroid taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re being discharged home. You’ve improved a lot—kidneys are fine, pain is controlled, and the flare is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Dr. Lee. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. You came in with abdominal pain and diarrhea—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it started about three days ago. Left side, really sharp and squeezing pain. I’ve been going to the bathroom like 20 times a day, some blood when I wipe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, low-grade. Nothing over 100, but I’ve been feeling feverish, especially this burning sensation that starts in my head and moves down my body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll keep an eye on that. You’re on prednisone for Crohn’s—were you increasing it before coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I bumped it to 30 mg. It wasn’t helping much, and I ran out of my Seroquel too—my anxiety’s been worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ve restarted your Seroquel. That should help with the anxiety. We’re also giving you IV fluids because your labs show dehydration and your kidney function is a bit off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My creatinine was 1.8, right? That’s not good. Is my kidney okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s elevated, but we think it’s due to dehydration and diarrhea—what we call pre-renal. With fluids, it should improve. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the pain? It’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Dilaudid in the ER and started IV steroids. We’ll keep managing your pain with IV meds for now. You’re NPO—nothing by mouth—for a few hours to let your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: NPO? How long will that be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just until we see if your symptoms start improving. We’ll reassess in the morning. We also did a CT scan to check for complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No blockage, no abscess, no free air. The contrast made it to your distal ileum, which is good. It looks like inflammation from a Crohn’s flare, not a surgical issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just a flare? But I’ve been on steroids for years. Why isn’t it getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Crohn’s can be tough. You’re steroid-dependent, which means your body relies on them, but they don’t always control flares completely. We’re using IV methylprednisolone now, which is stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my rash? I’ve got these itchy blisters on my arms and chest. I scratch them and they bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It could be related to your meds or immune system. We’ll send a note to dermatology, but right now, we’re focusing on the flare and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Creatinine is down to 1.4, and you’re more hydrated. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start you on clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance to a soft diet. We’re also switching you to oral pain meds—morphine tablets as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I hate the IV pain pump. What about the calcium? I saw it was high on my chart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your calcium was 10.7 on admission—slightly high. But it’s come down, and your PTH is low, which suggests it’s not from hyperparathyroidism. Vitamin D levels were low, so we’ll follow up on that with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. It’s likely related to your Crohn’s or steroid use. We’ll monitor it, but no treatment is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Creatinine is now 1.1, back to your baseline. You’re eating regular food and managing pain with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We want to make sure your pain is stable and you’re not having frequent bowel movements. Your stool tests came back—all negative for infection, C. diff, parasites. So it’s not infectious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the symptoms, history, and imaging all point to a flare. We’re stopping azathioprine for now since you had kidney issues with it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about long-term? I can’t keep doing this every few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss that with your gastroenterologist. There are other biologics we can consider. But for now, we’re focusing on getting you through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are almost all normal. Hemoglobin dropped a bit, but not enough to need a transfusion. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if things stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue prednisone—60 mg daily—and taper it by 5 mg each week. We’re sending you home with morphine for pain, pantoprazole for reflux, and your Seroquel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: 60 mg? That’s high. Won’t that cause more cataracts or other side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is high, but necessary to control the flare. That’s why we’re giving you a clear taper schedule. The longer you stay on high doses, the more side effects, so we want you to follow the taper exactly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the B12 shots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue monthly. We’ll coordinate with your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your vitamin D levels came back low. We’ll send a letter to your doctors so they can address it in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a factor. Low vitamin D is common in Crohn’s, especially with steroid use. Supplements may help, but we’ll leave that to your GI team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. You’re stable, eating well, and pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any final instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Keep taking prednisone as prescribed and taper weekly. Use morphine only as needed. Watch for fevers, worsening pain, or vomiting—those mean you should come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And smoking? I’ve cut down, but not quit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We strongly recommend quitting. Smoking makes Crohn’s worse and increases flares. Your cough and reduced urine output are likely tied to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Follow up with your GI doctor in one week. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you're here with abdominal pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same pain as last time, but worse. It's in the right lower side again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how’s your bowel movement? Any blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood, but I’ve had about 22 watery black stools in the last day. I don’t know why they’re black.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Black stools can mean digested blood, but it could also be from something you ate or medication. We’ll check that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t changed my diet. I’ve been eating even with the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also saw you had a cough and sweats. Are those still going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the sweats have been there for about a week. And I’ve got this cough with dark sputum, not bloody, but kind of blackish.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever. Just the sweats and the headache around my left eye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of Crohn’s disease, and the fact that you were just discharged five days ago, this sounds like a flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I was feeling better after the last hospital stay. Why is it back so soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes Crohn’s can relapse quickly, especially if the taper on steroids is too fast or if there’s ongoing inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 55 mg prednisone when I left. Is that not enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might not be. We’ll restart IV steroids to get better control. You’ll also get IV fluids since you’ve had a lot of diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—to let your gut rest. Once things settle, we’ll start you on liquids and then soft food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain? It’s pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you morphine in the ER, and we’ll continue pain meds through the IV. But we’ll avoid long-term opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to depend on them. But I need relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage it carefully. We also restarted your Imuran—azathioprine—to help control the immune response long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from before. It didn’t work well last time because of kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is normal now, so it should be safe. We’ll monitor your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the CT scan I had earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It showed mild inflammation around the sigmoid colon, but no blockage or abscess. It looks chronic, not new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not something else? Like an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool. No Salmonella, Shigella, C. diff, or other infections. So it’s likely your Crohn’s acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the sweats and cough? Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Your lungs are clear on exam. The sweats were there last time too, and no infection was found. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking better. You’ve had less pain overnight and only four loose stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the pain is more manageable. Can I try some food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids. If that goes well, we’ll move to a soft diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the IV steroids? How long will I be on those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you to oral prednisone tomorrow. You’ll take 50 mg daily and taper slowly as directed by your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope this time the taper doesn’t cause a relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make it slower this time. And staying on Imuran should help prevent flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been on a regular diet since yesterday with no issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. The sweats have stopped too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your labs are stable. WBC is still a bit high, but that’s expected with inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my vitamin D? I remember they said it was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re supposed to be on 800 IU daily. We’ve added a prescription for 400 IU twice a day to make it easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that enough? Should I get more sun?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The supplement should help. But quitting smoking would do more for your overall health and Crohn’s control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I know. I’ve tried patches before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can set you up with another patch and counseling. It really does make a difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re planning for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Prednisone 10 mg daily—take five tablets, then reduce by one tablet each week. Also, continue Imuran 50 mg daily, pantoprazole, and quetiapine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No opioids. If you need relief, use acetaminophen. We want to avoid dependency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vitamin D?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, two capsules a day—400 IU each. Take it with food for better absorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to get labs done before seeing my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, check CBC and liver tests one day before your appointment. Fax the results to her office.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if my symptoms come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have worsening pain, vomiting, fever over 101, or dark or bloody stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve responded well. Keep up with your meds, the lab work, and follow-up. And please consider the smoking cessation program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I've been reviewing your case. You came in today with left lower quadrant abdominal pain and increased bowel movements. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the pain started yesterday—sharp and throbbing in the lower left side. I’ve been having about 14 loose stools a day, which is way more than normal for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned in the ER that you increased your Imuran dose to 75mg because of the looser stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I’ve done that before when things flare up. I usually talk to Dr. Patel, but I thought I could manage it on my own this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but we need to be careful with self-adjusting medications, especially Imuran. It can affect your blood counts. We’ve started you on IV methylprednisolone to help with the inflammation from your Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is that like the prednisone I take at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very similar—just stronger and given through the IV for now. We also restarted IV Imuran, but we’ll watch your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had issues with Imuran before, right? My kidneys didn’t like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s correct. You had acute kidney injury in the past, so we’re monitoring your kidney function and blood counts daily. For now, we’re keeping you on it, but we’ll adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. The pain’s pretty bad—can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we gave you a small dose of hydromorphone earlier. We’re setting up a PCA pump so you can control the pain safely. But we’ll avoid long-term opioids because of your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get that. I’ve had problems with them before. But this pain is different—it’s spreading to the right side now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’re concerned about whether this could be a kidney stone, especially with your history. We’ll do an ultrasound and an abdominal X-ray to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I haven’t had a stone in years, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still, we want to rule it out. No fever or chills, right? And your last stool was brown and loose—no blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever. Stool was brown, no blood that I saw.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We tested your stool—no infection like C. diff, salmonella, or parasites. So this looks like a Crohn’s flare, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it was something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your imaging from yesterday. The kidney ultrasound was normal—no stones or swelling. The abdominal X-ray showed mildly dilated bowel loops, but given your past surgery, it’s hard to tell if that’s significant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a kidney stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, doesn’t look like it. The pain radiating to your right testicle might be referred pain from the bowel inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s weird, but okay. What about the Imuran? How’s my blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelet count has been dropping. It’s down to 108, which is below your normal. We think Imuran might be causing this—thrombocytopenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it keeps dropping. So we’ve decided to stop Imuran. Your platelets should recover. We’ve consulted your gastroenterologist, Dr. Patel, and she agrees.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now? I still need something for Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Dr. Patel and her colleague are planning to start you on a new immunomodulatory agent as an outpatient. We’ll discuss that at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. What about the antibiotics? I was on cipro before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched you to rifaximin briefly, but since you didn’t feel it helped, we’re going back to ciprofloxacin. You’ll take it for three months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I prefer cipro. It works better for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelet count is already improving—up to 135 today. That’s a good sign stopping Imuran helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. How’s the inflammation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still seeing some tenderness, especially in the lower abdomen. But your CRP is normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds—are we still using the PCA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re transitioning you to oral MSContin and MSIR. You said it helped better than the IV dilaudid, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. Less foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also tried tizanidine for muscle spasms, but it didn’t seem to help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t notice anything. Maybe not needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRI of your abdomen today. It shows stable inflammation in the sigmoid colon—no abscess or stricture. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery or drainage needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at this time. The inflammation is chronic but stable. The main issue was the flare and the drop in platelets from Imuran.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll start a new Crohn’s med soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with Dr. Patel. She’ll coordinate that. For now, you’re on prednisone, cipro, and a PPI for your reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Protonix at home. Now it’s pantoprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same class—just switched to pantoprazole IV, now oral. You’ll take it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is better, eating normally, and your platelets are back to normal. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I get pain meds for home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not prescribing opioids. Dr. Patel strongly advised against it due to your history. But your oral meds are helping, and the pain should continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I don’t want to go back to that. I’ll stick with the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your labs are stable, you’re ambulating well, and your pain is manageable. Discharge is set for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about smoking? I’m still on the patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using the 7mg nicotine patch. Smoking worsens Crohn’s, so quitting is really important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll keep trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds am I taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ciprofloxacin twice daily for three months, pantoprazole twice daily, and prednisone—three tablets daily, which you’ll taper down as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No Imuran?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct, it was stopped due to low platelets. Your GI team will start a new medication soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no opioids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, but your pain is much better, and we’re confident the oral meds will keep it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with Dr. Patel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’ll contact you. Also, keep using the nicotine patch and avoid self-adjusting any meds, especially Seroquel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve had this sharp pain in my lower left abdomen again—same as before. Started the day after I went out to dinner. I also had watery bowel movements all night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea, vomiting, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I don’t think I had a fever, but I felt sweaty. One of my friends who was at dinner also got diarrhea, so I wonder if it was something we ate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Given your history of Crohn’s disease, we always have to check if this is a flare, but a sick contact makes infection possible too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was doing well until this. I’m still on prednisone and Imuran. Is this another flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think so yet. Your vitals are stable, and your exam shows tenderness in the left lower quadrant, but no guarding or rebound—so no signs of serious complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But the pain is pretty bad. I needed Dilaudid in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve given you IV Dilaudid for pain. We’ll keep monitoring and may switch to oral meds as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should we do another MRI? I had one last month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding repeat imaging since your last MRI was recent and showed stable inflammation without abscess or stricture. We don’t want to overexpose you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about tests for infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent a stool sample. It’s being checked for bacteria like Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, and also parasites and C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what do you think it is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, it looks more like viral gastroenteritis—especially with your friend also sick. But we’ll confirm once we get the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool results came back. No Salmonella, Shigella, C. diff, or parasites. All negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection? But I had diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a virus. Those don’t show up on these tests. The fact that your friend is sick too supports that idea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So not a Crohn’s flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think so. Your CRP and ESR came back normal—those are markers of inflammation. If it were a flare, we’d expect them to be high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The virus can cause intestinal irritation and spasms, especially with your history of bowel surgery. We’ll manage the pain while your body recovers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Imuran for a while. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding it for now. Your platelet count is a bit low—158, which is mild, but we don’t want it to drop further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that before, right? Last time I was here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Azathioprine can cause low platelets. We’ll restart it only if your counts improve at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And prednisone—I’m still on 20mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping you on 20mg daily. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still some ache, but not as sharp. I haven’t had diarrhea since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to switch your pain med to oral Dilaudid and reduce the dose gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m glad I don’t need IV meds anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also consulted Pain Management. They recommend starting two new medications: tizanidine and Lyrica.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do they do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tizanidine helps with muscle spasms, which can contribute to abdominal pain. Lyrica is for nerve-related pain and may help with your chronic discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of Lyrica. Is it addictive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not addictive like opioids, but it can cause drowsiness. We’ll start low and monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. What about my stomach? I’ve been feeling more heartburn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you from Protonix to pantoprazole. Same type of medication—just a change in brand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable, and your pain is much improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll go home on prednisone, pantoprazole, loperamide as needed, and the new pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Imuran?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still holding it. Your platelets are stable but not up enough yet. Follow up with your GI doctor to recheck blood work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new pain meds—how do I take them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tizanidine—one at bedtime, can increase to twice daily if needed. Lyrica—start once daily, can go to twice after three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a small supply—only for breakthrough pain. Use it sparingly and avoid alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. So final diagnosis was viral infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—viral gastroenteritis. Not a Crohn’s flare. Your labs and symptoms support that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I follow up with GI and Pain Management?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call both offices to schedule. Especially important to check your platelets before restarting Imuran.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I ate some sausage patties yesterday, and about three hours later, I started vomiting—six times—and had 20 watery bowel movements. The pain in my left side is way worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And this feels different from your usual Crohn’s flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s sharper, especially in my left flank. It gets worse when I move or have a bowel movement. I’ve had Crohn’s for years, but this is more intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You were given fluids and pain meds in the ER. Your labs show high white blood cells and your kidney function is off—creatinine is 2.0, which is elevated from your baseline of 1.1. We think you’re dehydrated, which may have triggered acute kidney injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I haven’t been eating much. I lost about seven pounds recently—no car, so I’ve been relying on the food pantry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely contribute. We’ll give you IV fluids to help your kidneys and rehydrate you. We’re also checking stool tests to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had something like this a few weeks ago. They said it was infectious diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your record shows that. This time, we’re being cautious. GI will see you in the morning, but for now, we’ll keep you on bowel rest and monitor your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m on prednisone—15 mg daily—but I haven’t been taking my B12 shot in three months. Can’t afford the supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a B12 injection while you’re here. Your level came back normal, but we don’t want it dropping. We’ll also restart your regular meds as you tolerate food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back—all negative. No C. diff, no parasites, no bacteria like Salmonella or E. coli.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from what we can tell. Given your history, this still looks like a Crohn’s flare, possibly triggered by the meal. We’re starting you on ciprofloxacin just in case there’s a low-grade bacterial component.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to some antibiotics—Flagyl, Zofran, gabapentin. Is cipro safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, cipro is not on your allergy list. We’ll monitor you closely. We’re also increasing your prednisone to 40 mg to help control the flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being on high-dose steroids. I get blurry vision and mood swings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll taper it slowly—down by 5 mg each week—so your body can adjust. You’ve been on it long-term, so we can’t stop it suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. What about my pain? Lyrica and tizanidine were helping before this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on both. We lowered the tizanidine dose to 2 mg every six hours to avoid drowsiness. Lyrica is now 50 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your kidneys this morning. No stones or blockage. Both kidneys are around 10 cm—normal size, no hydronephrosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had kidney stones before, so I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that in your history. But this time, it’s not the cause. Your flank pain is likely from the Crohn’s inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count has dropped from 20.3 to 5.6—great improvement. Your creatinine is now 1.4, so your kidneys are recovering with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’m feeling less nauseous and my stomach isn’t cramping as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on a clear liquid diet and slowly advance it. If you tolerate it, you might be able to eat solid food tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have toast or soup?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s start with broth and jello today. If no vomiting or diarrhea, we’ll try toast tomorrow. Small steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, I’ve got this rash on my arms and chest. It’s been there for a few months. Is it from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like erythematous papules—possibly related to chronic inflammation or medication. Since it’s not new or worsening, we’ll monitor it. Not urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It itches sometimes. Should I use lotion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fragrance-free moisturizer should be fine. Let the nurse know if it gets worse or starts oozing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been on solids since yesterday with no issues. Your last creatinine was 1.2—back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re stable. You’ll finish your 10-day course of cipro—six more days. And we’re giving you a B12 shot before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still can’t afford calcium and vitamin D. But I know I need them with long-term steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing chewable calcium and vitamin D. Social work is helping you get a pharmacy card so you can pick them up at a discount.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team reviewed your case. They agree this was a Crohn’s flare, not an abscess or perforation. No need for repeat imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re healing well. We’ll keep you on pantoprazole twice daily to protect your stomach from steroid effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need narcotics for pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re not discharging you on narcotics. Your pain is improving with Lyrica and tizanidine. We’ve adjusted the doses to help with both nerve pain and muscle spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I don’t want to get dependent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. Your vitals are stable, you’re eating well, and labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the cipro—six more days. Taper your prednisone slowly: 40 mg for two more days, then reduce by 5 mg each week until you’re back to 15 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take calcium and vitamin D daily. Lyrica twice daily, tizanidine every six hours as needed. And get your B12 shot monthly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have follow-ups with GI and pain clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both are scheduled. Call us if you develop fever, severe pain, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. A social worker will give you a ride card to get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—I take 4 prednisone tablets today and tomorrow, then 3.5 next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We wrote it out clearly on your discharge sheet. Each week, reduce by half a tablet until you’re at 1.5 tablets daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cipro is twice a day with food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every 12 hours. Don’t skip doses. It’s important to finish the full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Keep up with your follow-ups and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid certain foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, stick to low-residue foods—white rice, toast, bananas. Avoid fatty or spicy meals. We’ll discuss long-term diet with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re ready to go home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will bring your prescriptions and discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted this morning for worsening diarrhea and abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, thanks. So for the past few days, my bowel movements went from about 6 a day to every hour. They’re watery, yellow-green, no blood, but I’ve seen a little on the toilet paper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a low-grade fever, like 100.3, the morning before I came in. And my left lower belly pain is sharp and crampy. It’s worse now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You also mentioned pain in your left testicle and flank. Can you describe that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the testicle pain started right before I came to the ER. It feels heavy, like a pulling. I only have one testicle—I had the left one removed years ago. And my back, left side, hurts too. I’ve had kidney stones before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for that. We’ll check for infection and inflammation. We’ve started IV fluids because your labs show mild dehydration and your kidney function is a bit off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney okay? Last time I was in, my creatinine was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.3, up from your baseline of 1.1. But it’s likely due to dehydration from the diarrhea. We’re giving fluids, and it should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ve been on prednisone for years. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re actually increasing it to 40 mg daily because we suspect a Crohn’s flare. We’ve also started IV steroids and an antibiotic, ciprofloxacin, just in case there’s infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to Flagyl and Zofran. Are you using those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re avoiding those. You’re on ciprofloxacin, which you’ve taken before without issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Also, I’ve been feeling pins and needles in my left foot and up to my knee. Started in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It could be related to nerve irritation from the abdominal inflammation or part of your chronic back pain. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and parasites. No infection found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely yes. Your CT scan shows thickening at the anastomosis site—consistent with Crohn’s flare. We also saw a small 2-mm kidney stone in your left kidney, but it’s not blocking anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the back and testicle pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The stone might have passed and caused referred pain. Your scrotal ultrasound showed no torsion, but there is an enlarged vessel in the left groin. We’ll follow up on that with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really uncomfortable. Can I get something for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re giving IV hydromorphone for now. We’ll adjust as your pain improves. We also restarted your quetiapine for anxiety—you weren’t taking it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot. I’ve been stressed. A close friend’s been going through a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll help manage your anxiety while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRI enterography confirms active Crohn’s disease in the distal ileum—about 7-8 cm of inflamed bowel. No abscess or complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So same as before. No surgery needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at this time. Medication should control it. We’re planning a sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to get biopsies and confirm the flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to be sedated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be lightly sedated. It’s a short procedure. After that, we can start you on food again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry. Been on IV fluids too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Once the scope is done and we confirm it’s safe, we’ll advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The sigmoidoscopy showed ulceration and inflammation at the anastomosis. Biopsies confirm active inflammation. No infection in the tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So definitely a flare. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you from IV to oral prednisone. You’ll continue 40 mg daily until you speak with your GI doctor. We’re also sending you home with a 10-day course of oral ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. Your diarrhea has slowed, and you’re tolerating a regular diet. We’ll keep you one more day to make sure your pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My back pain is still bothering me. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing a lidocaine patch and cyclobenzaprine for muscle spasms. Avoid driving or alcohol—they can make you drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already on tizanidine at night. Should I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping tizanidine because cyclobenzaprine is similar. Taking both could increase sedation. Use the new meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today look better. White count is down, kidney function stable. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the pins and needles in my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still likely related to nerve irritation from the flare. It should improve as inflammation decreases. Let us know if it worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed some scabs on my chest and tattoos. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. Probably minor skin irritation. We’re giving you bacitracin ointment to apply as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. Your symptoms have improved, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue prednisone 40 mg daily until you talk to your GI doctor—they’ll guide the taper. Take ciprofloxacin twice daily for 10 days. Use the lidocaine patch and cyclobenzaprine as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hydromorphone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take one tablet every 6 hours as needed for severe pain. Don’t exceed that. And call your PCP about the enlarged groin vessel seen on ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be on any infection prevention? I’m on a lot of steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Discuss Bactrim prophylaxis with your doctor. It can help prevent infections when on long-term steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my B12 shot? I’m overdue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule that with your PCP. Keep up with monthly injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll follow up with GI and my regular doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And if diarrhea worsens, fever returns, or pain increases, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right track. Keep hydrated, rest, and take your meds as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid pork and broccoli? I ate those before this started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They might have triggered it. Stick to your usual diet for now and reintroduce foods slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.
