conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned ankle pain yesterday. How’s it doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better. It was both ankles, especially in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned the cipro might have caused tendon inflammation. We’ve stopped it. The pain could also be plantar fasciitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not on cipro anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’ll rely on bowel rest and hydration now. Your infection workup was negative, so antibiotics aren’t needed long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We swabbed the rash from your back. It grew coagulase-negative staph, but that’s likely just skin flora, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We’ll treat it topically. I’m prescribing mupirocin cream and a benzoyl peroxide wash to prevent spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is down to 1.3—kidney function is improving. And your pain is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in the next two days. You’ll go home on loperamide for diarrhea and hydromorphone for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Tysabri?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your infusion is still scheduled for next week. Your GI doctor will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have fever, severe pain, or more than 6 bloody stools a day. Also, if the ankle pain comes back, avoid heavy activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the kidney stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Drink plenty of water. You should pass it soon. If the pain gets worse, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking the pantoprazole for your GERD, and the quetiapine if your anxiety flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with GI and orthopedics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both within the next two weeks. And avoid Flexeril and ciprofloxacin—they’re now on your allergy list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having this sharp pain in my left side, like my old kidney stones. It started around 3 p.m. today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you notice anything else, like blood in your urine or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw blood in my urine after I got to the ER. But no fever or chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your vitals are stable now. We did an ultrasound of your kidneys. It didn’t show any stones or swelling, but we couldn’t see a normal urine flow from your left kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no stone? But the pain feels just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible the stone has already passed or is too small to see. The pain and blood in your urine suggest a kidney stone episode. We also noticed your creatinine is a bit high—1.4—so your kidneys aren’t filtering as well right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidney function dropped last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but likely due to dehydration from the pain and not drinking much. We’re giving you IV fluids to help. That usually brings the numbers back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I haven’t been eating or drinking much because of the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you some pain medication, and you should start feeling better. We’ll keep you on fluids overnight to support your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your creatinine has improved to 1.2. That’s a good sign your kidneys are recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the stone gone then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We still don’t see a stone on ultrasound, but based on your symptoms and history, we believe this was a kidney stone episode. The blood in your urine has cleared, which is another good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had these stones before. Last time, they said it was ammonium urate. Could this be the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s likely. Ammonium urate stones can form when the urine is too acidic. We want to prevent more stones by making your urine less acidic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do we do that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on a medication called potassium citrate. It helps make your urine more alkaline, which reduces the chance of these stones forming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it. Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people tolerate it well. We’ll monitor your potassium level to make sure it stays in a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain has improved, and you’re tolerating food and fluids. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain is much better. I’m glad I can eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on IV fluids a bit longer, but you’re moving in the right direction. Your Crohn’s seems stable—no diarrhea or abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, my stomach’s been fine. Just the flank pain this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll continue your usual medications for Crohn’s and anxiety as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your latest creatinine is down to 1.1, and your potassium is normal. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if things keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I need to stay on the potassium citrate long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. You’ll take it three times a day with meals. It’s key to preventing more stones, especially since you’ve had ammonium urate stones before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should drink more water too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. At least two liters a day. More if it’s hot or you’re active. That helps flush out your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your case, and you’re doing well. No more pain, labs are stable, and you’re eating normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Just want to make sure I don’t have another episode like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help prevent that. You’ll go home with potassium citrate and instructions to stay hydrated. Your primary doctor will check your potassium and creatinine this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I avoid anything else? Like certain foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For ammonium urate stones, it helps to limit animal proteins like red meat and shellfish. A diet lower in purines can reduce stone risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll talk to a dietitian too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’re cleared to go home today. You’re alert, walking fine, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll take the potassium citrate as prescribed and drink plenty of fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and call your doctor if you have pain, blood in urine, or swelling. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointment for lab work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my back pain has been acting up. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam shows chronic back pain, likely from long-standing issues. As long as it’s manageable and not getting worse, it’s okay for now. Keep using your usual methods for relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll stick with heat and stretching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And remember, avoid NSAIDs—they can hurt your kidneys and stomach, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’ll use acetaminophen instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set for discharge. The nurse will give you your prescriptions and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay hydrated and follow up on those labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. My back’s been hurting too—same old problem, I think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll address that. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids and some Dilaudid for pain. Let’s see how you do tonight.

conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.text: Same as before, then?

conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried gabapentin and others—didn’t help. But tizanidine might be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids again? I’ve had cataracts and other side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This will be a short course, quickly tapered by your doctor. The goal is to stop the flare so you don’t end up with complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust your judgment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking better. Your pain is down, and your stools are less frequent—only about 8 today, and more formed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel like I’m turning a corner. Still tired, but the urgency is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll keep you on prednisone, tizanidine, and your usual pantoprazole. We’re switching to oral Percocet for back pain as we taper IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to keep taking Percocet at home?

conversation_lines.text: Got it. No driving. What about my Tysabri and B12 shots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue both monthly. Your specialist will coordinate the next infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray today shows no pneumonia—just a dry cough, probably from the steroids. Everything else is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been coughing a bit, but no fever. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your Crohn’s is calming down, and your back pain is manageable. We’re planning for discharge in a couple days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Stools are nearly normal—only 4 today. Pain is mild. We’ll finalize your discharge plan tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.text: You’ll take prednisone 50 mg daily—same dose—for now. Your specialist will call to taper it. Also, Percocet as needed, tizanidine three times a day, pantoprazole, Tums, B12, and Tysabri as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’ll follow up with your GI doctor for the steroid taper and with spine clinic for your back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another MRI or procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll keep hydrated and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Remember: no driving with Percocet and tizanidine, no alcohol, and take prednisone as directed until your doctor calls to taper it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for helping me through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.text: A blockage? But I’ve had surgeries before. Is that from scar tissue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. With your history of multiple abdominal surgeries, adhesions are a common cause. But we also have to consider your Crohn’s disease causing inflammation or a stricture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Tysabri for a few months now. I thought that was helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be helping overall, but flare-ups can still happen. We’ll need more imaging to see what’s going on. We’re going to do a CT scan tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery is a last resort. Right now, we’re hoping this resolves with medical management. Surgery was consulted and agrees—serial exams for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. The pain is really bad. Oxycodone didn’t help much earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you IV Dilaudid, which is stronger. We’ll keep adjusting your pain meds. We also gave ondansetron for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want the pain to settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan from last night showed persistent inflammation in the distal ileum—about 6–7 cm thickened segment. Mild dilation just above it, but no complete obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s my Crohn’s acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s likely contributing to the partial blockage. The bowel is inflamed and narrowed, slowing things down. But no abscess or perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dark stools? Is there bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tested negative for blood. The dark color might be from slower transit or something you ate—like the cheese last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t passed much gas either. Feels like I need to, but nothing comes out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with a partial obstruction. We’re going to place an NG tube to decompress your stomach and help relieve symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I refused it in the ER, but if it helps, okay. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use it intermittently—only when needed. It should help with nausea and bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat X-ray shows the bowel dilation is still there—about 5.3 cm—but no worsening. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And your labs show no infection—CRP and ESR are normal, C. diff and cultures negative, CMV not detected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my kidney numbers? I saw my creatinine was up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine went from 1.1 to 1.4. Likely due to dehydration. We’ve been giving IV fluids, and it’s already back down to 1.1.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been anxious—pain makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started quetiapine and low-dose lorazepam to help. But you became a bit confused last night, so we stopped the lorazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel foggy. I’d rather be alert, even if anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the quetiapine and focus on pain control. We’re switching you to oral Dilaudid as you’re tolerating sips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your NG tube has been helping. You’re passing more gas now, and your abdomen is less tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better. Still sore, but not as intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO for now, but plan to start clear liquids tomorrow if this trend continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re starting on clear liquids today. Your bowel sounds are better, and you passed gas overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I eat real food soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance slowly. If you tolerate liquids, we’ll try soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MR enterography results are back. There’s a 10 cm segment of active inflammation in the distal ileum, but it’s stable compared to your last scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No new damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No abscess, fistula, or definite stricture. The bowel dilation has actually improved since the CT. That’s a positive sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the treatment is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Rest, IV fluids, pain control, and bowel rest are helping. We’ll remove the NG tube today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to get rid of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on a regular diet since yesterday and no issues. Pain is much better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, manageable with oral meds. I’m feeling more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home tomorrow. You’ll go home on Percocet for breakthrough pain, same prednisone dose, and continue Tysabri monthly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another hospital stay like this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not. Staying on Tysabri and following up with GI should help prevent flares. Your gastroenterologist’s office will call to schedule your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking quetiapine as prescribed. Talk to your PCP if anxiety worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vitals are stable, labs improved, and you’re walking and eating normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Take Percocet only as needed, not while driving. Keep your primary care and GI follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well, and call if pain returns or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I’ve been reviewing your case. You came in last night with abdominal pain and frequent diarrhea—can you tell me more about how it started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it started around midnight. I had this sharp pain in my lower left side, coming in waves. Then I went to the bathroom eight times between 2 and 3 a.m.—all watery, no blood in the stool, but I saw blood on the toilet paper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you said this feels similar to past Crohn’s flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Not like my kidney stone pain—it doesn’t go to my back or groin. This is more like the cramping I’ve had before when my Crohn’s acts up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. You also mentioned you’ve been off prednisone for about a week. That might be a trigger. We’re going to run some tests to rule out infection and check your inflammation levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been on Tysabri for a few months now. Should I still get my next dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were due for it today, but we’re holding off until we confirm this is a flare and not an infection. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work came back. White count is normal, no sign of infection. CRP is slightly elevated at 4.5, which suggests inflammation. Blood cultures are negative so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably Crohn’s again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks that way. Your kidney function is a bit off—creatinine is 1.3, up from your baseline of 1.1. That’s likely from dehydration due to the diarrhea. We’re giving you IV fluids to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray of your abdomen is back. Good news—no sign of a blockage or obstruction. Bowel gas pattern is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about another surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll avoid that if we can. The plan is to treat this as a Crohn’s flare. We’re starting you on IV steroids—solumedrol every eight hours—to reduce the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to go back on prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once we transition from IV. We’ll start you on 40 mg daily. We also want to do a flexible sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to confirm the flare and take biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Biopsies? Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. It’s important to make sure it’s active inflammation and not an infection like CMV. Your CMV serologies came back negative, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scope went well. We saw ulceration and inflammation in the rectosigmoid and ileum—classic Crohn’s pattern. We took biopsies from both areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And it’s definitely Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The preliminary read shows chronic active ileitis with ulceration—very consistent with Crohn’s. No granulomas or dysplasia. We’ll also start you on hydrocortisone enemas nightly to target the rectal inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using loperamide, but it’s not helping much with the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it on board for symptom control, but the steroids and enemas should reduce the inflammation causing the diarrhea. We’ll hold off on antibiotics since stool C. diff was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still some tenderness in the lower left side, but not the waves of pain I had. I slept through the night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Your creatinine is down to 1.1—kidneys are recovering with fluids. We’ll keep the IVs going a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re advancing your diet to clear liquids today. If that goes well, we’ll move to low-residue solids tomorrow. Avoid anything too fibrous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look stable. Hemoglobin is 12.5, slightly down but not concerning. Platelets and white count are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit tired. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but also from the flare and being NPO. As you start eating and the inflammation calms, your energy should improve. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is minimal, you’re tolerating food, and your labs are improving. We’re switching you from IV solumedrol to oral prednisone—same 40 mg dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on this long-term again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting at 40 mg, but you’ll taper it down with your GI doctor. The goal is to get you off, but we need to control this flare first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about Tysabri? I’m worried about stopping it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held this dose, but GI thinks it’s safe to restart as an outpatient. You’ll follow up with them in a week to decide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed this rash on my left leg—it’s itchy and I keep scratching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that—some excoriations and dried blood. It looks like a chronic eczematous rash. We’ll give you bacitracin ointment to prevent infection and suggest you avoid scratching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. It’s been bothering me for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. Your pain is much better, you’re eating well, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take prednisone 40 mg daily, tapering as directed by GI. Continue the hydrocortisone enema every night for 18 more days. For pain, you’ll have extended-release morphine twice daily for three days, and oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—omeprazole twice daily, loperamide four times daily, and your monthly B12 injection. Apply bacitracin to the rash twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll call to schedule within the week. They’ll decide on continuing Tysabri and your steroid taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone as needed. But if you have fever, worsening pain, or heavy bleeding, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid any foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to low-residue for now—white bread, rice, bananas. Avoid raw veggies, nuts, and seeds until your GI appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll keep a food log.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent idea. That’ll help your GI team adjust your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the enemas—I use them at bedtime, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every night. They help reduce rectal inflammation. You should notice less bleeding and urgency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. That was scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re on the mend. Just follow the plan, and you’ll keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had bad stomach pain for about two days now, and a lot of diarrhea. It feels like one of my usual Crohn’s flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I see you have a history of Crohn’s disease and several past surgeries. Is this pain similar to previous flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly like before. The diarrhea slowed this morning, but now the pain is more crampy. That usually happens when things slow down—my anatomy makes it hard to pass stool during flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned manual disimpaction doesn’t help much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. It never works for me. Usually, IV fluids help it pass on its own after a day or so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from tonight. There’s some fecal loading in the distal ileum and mild inflammation, but actually, it looks improved compared to your last scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, I guess. But why the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain is likely from the flare itself—your bowel is inflamed and the backed-up stool is stretching the area. But no obstruction, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I didn’t take the IV steroid they offered in the ER—was that a mistake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. We’re going to start you on 40 mg of oral prednisone daily. That’s a higher dose than you were on, and it should help calm the flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only on 5 mg before. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for a short time. Your GI doctor will taper it down later. We’re also giving IV fluids to rehydrate you and help the stool move through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit weak. My labs okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function was a bit off when you arrived—creatinine was 1.5, up from your baseline of 1.0. But that’s likely from dehydration. We’re fixing that with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the acidosis I saw on the board? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your bicarbonate was low at 13, but no anion gap and lactate was normal. It’s a metabolic acidosis from losing bicarbonate in diarrhea. We’re replacing it with IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not long-term. It should correct as you rehydrate. We’ll check your labs again in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I just reviewed your morning labs. Your creatinine is already down to 1.3, and bicarbonate is up to 18. That’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. My pain is also a lot better. I had a small bowel movement this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’re going to advance your diet to regular food today—lunch and dinner—if you can tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I stop the IV fluids then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep them going for now, but if you eat and drink well, we can remove them later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stool test came back—no C. diff, no parasites, no salmonella or shigella. Infection is unlikely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything points to a flare. We’re stopping the Cipro since we don’t think it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound to check for a hernia, since your pain is in the lower right. Good news—it’s negative. No hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that. Thanks for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are almost back to normal—creatinine is 0.9, bicarbonate is 23. You’re euvolemic and tolerating food well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. You’ll continue the 40 mg prednisone daily until you see your GI doctor—they’ll taper it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain? I might need something for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing a short course of oxycodone for breakthrough pain—take as needed, up to four times a day, but only if necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep taking omeprazole, B12 injections, and Tysabri. Loperamide only if diarrhea returns. And quetiapine at night if you need help sleeping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the urine and stool cultures still be checked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’re still pending, but we’ll follow up. If anything comes back positive, someone will contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep drinking fluids, take your meds, and follow up with GI soon. We’ll get you set up to go home in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really bad stomach pain and diarrhea. It started a few hours after I ate at a cookout yesterday.

conversation_lines.text: I see. How often are you having bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Every 30 minutes or so. And I can see undigested food in the stool. No blood, though.

conversation_lines.text: Got it. You were just discharged a week ago for a Crohn’s flare—does this pain feel different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We did a renal ultrasound in the ER—no stones. But we’ll check a CT to be sure nothing’s changed with your Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been on prednisone since last time—should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just don’t want to go through another flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do everything we can. For now, we’re giving IV fluids and some pain medication to keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs came back—white count is normal, and markers of inflammation like CRP and ESR are low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s good, right? Not a Crohn’s flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Those markers are usually high during a flare. This suggests it’s less likely to be active Crohn’s inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what’s causing the pain and diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still working on that. Your CT is scheduled for tomorrow. But given the timing after the cookout, we’re thinking it could be gastroenteritis—maybe a viral infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like food poisoning? But I only ate a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t take much. Viruses can be very contagious. And with your history, your gut might react more strongly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I have results from your CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. There’s no abscess, no obstruction, and no new inflammation. In fact, the area of thickened bowel from your Crohn’s looks better than last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The CT confirms it’s not a flare. The pain and diarrhea are likely from a gastrointestinal infection—gastroenteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.text: Probably not. Most cases are viral and get better on their own. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids and let your body heal.

conversation_lines.text: I tried a little broth earlier. Felt okay. Can I eat more?

conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that didn’t go well. How long should I stay on liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit better, but still crampy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing the pain. But the trend is positive. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. What should I do at home?
